issue: The figure encodes the KV write one decode step too early and contains an off-by-one token label. It shows token1 (sampled by prefill) and token2 (sampled by the first decode) being appended in the same step they are sampled, and labels token n as 'nth decode' even though token2 is labeled 'first decode'. This contradicts the caption's 'one step after it is sampled' and the prose on p. 14 that a token's K/V enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not the step in which it is sampled.
evidence: Caption: 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' p. 14: 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' Figure labels: 'token1 from prefill' -> append K/V; 'token2 first decode' -> append K/V; '... token n nth decode' -> append K/V.
acceptance_test: Relabel or annotate the figure so the append arrows are offset by one step: prompt tokens append during prefill; token1 (prefill output) appends at first decode; token2 (first decode output) appends at second decode; ... token n appends at nth decode. Remove the 'token n nth decode' label or renumber tokens so token2 is not both 'first decode' and appended at first decode. Verify the rendered figure matches the caption and p. 14 timing convention.

figure: Figure 1.1 (The KV cache: single-layer detail view)
issue: The left-column step labels are off by one relative to the KV-write timing rule that the same caption and Ch. 2 state as a key detail, so the figure permits the wrong inference that a generated token's K/V is appended in the step that sampled it. Each of the four token boxes (token1 / from prefill, token2 / first decode, token3 / second decode, ... token_n / nth decode) has a rightward arrow into the orange 'append K/V per layer·head' box, making the sub-label read as the step in which that token's K/V is appended. But the caption says 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt-token K/V is written during prefill', and printed p.14 (§2) states 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' token1 is the first sampled (generated) token, so its K/V is appended in the first decode step (when token1 is the input), not in prefill; likewise token2's K/V is appended in the second decode step, not the first. The figure's labels therefore tie each generated token to the step that produced it, not the step that appends it. Note the contrast with Figure 2.1 (PDF 35 / printed 15), which correctly gives the first token no 'populate' arrow into the cache (only the green 'initialize' arrow into decode), i.e. it does not claim the first token's K/V is written in prefill.
evidence: Caption (PDF 27): 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled; prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' Figure left column: 'token1 / from prefill', 'token2 / first decode', 'token3 / second decode', '... token_n / nth decode', each with an arrow into 'append K/V per layer·head'. §2 (PDF 34 / printed 14): 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' Under the figure's visual logic (token box -> append box, sub-label = step), token1's append is placed in prefill, contradicting the rule; the same off-by-one applies to token2/token3/token_n (each generated token is labeled with its sampling step, not its append step).
acceptance_test: After the fix, a reader using only the figure plus its caption must be able to state that (a) the prefill step appends the prompt tokens' K/V, and (b) each generated token's K/V is appended in the step in which that token is the input (one step after it is sampled) — i.e. token1 in the first decode step, token2 in the second, etc. Concretely, either relabel the left rows to the append step (prefill row = prompt tokens; first-decode row = token1; second-decode row = token2; nth-decode row = token_{n-1}) so the token feeding 'append K/V' in a row is the input of that row's step, or keep the production-step labels but add explicit 'sampled in X -> appended in Y' text per row. Verify that no row pairs a generated token with the step that sampled it as that token's append step, and that the figure no longer conflicts with Figure 2.1's treatment of the first token.

figure: Figure 1.1 — KV cache detail view (token -> append K/V -> stored K / stored V -> read for attention)
issue: The drawing does not encode the one-step delay between sampling a generated token and writing its K/V. The figure alone therefore supports an off-by-one reading that the caption explicitly forbids, and the caption's central distinction is carried entirely by prose rather than by the diagram.
evidence: Caption (printed p. 7): 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled: prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' Figure labels: 'token1 / from prefill', 'token2 / first decode', 'token3 / second decode', '... token_n / nth decode', each with an identical arrow into the orange box 'append K/V per layer-head'. Nothing in the drawing distinguishes 'token sampled at step t' from 'token processed as input at step t+1'; the prefill token and the decode tokens are drawn with the same arrow semantics and the same box treatment. A reader scanning the figure can conclude that each decode step appends the K/V of the token it just sampled, which is wrong by one step.
acceptance_test: Redraw so write timing is legible without the caption: label the append arrows 'written during prefill' (token1) and 'written at step t+1' (token2, token3), or add a step axis / step counter to the token column. Acceptance: a reader shown only the figure (caption obscured) states correctly that a generated token's K/V is written one step after it is sampled, and that prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.

figure: Figure 1.1 — secondary annotations ('from prefill', 'first decode', 'second decode', 'nth decode', 'layer L . h1...h_h', 'next token q')
issue: The smallest in-figure annotations appear to fall at or below the 8 pt print floor, and they carry essential semantics (which token is which; which layer/head the stored tensors belong to; what the query is).
evidence: At 150 dpi the secondary annotation glyphs render at roughly 0.6-0.7x the x-height of the 10.5 pt body text set on the same page (compare 'not the expert count: GQA/MQA shrink the per-token KV width...' immediately below the caption). 'layer L . h1...h_h' and 'next token q' are the smallest and are the least redundant strings in the figure: they are the only place the reader learns the cache is indexed per (layer, head) and that the attention step consumes a query. The primary labels ('token1', 'append K/V', 'stored K - keys', 'read for attention') are visibly larger and legible.
acceptance_test: Measure the smallest annotation at 100% on the printed page, or extract font sizes from the figure source: every figure glyph, including 'layer L . h1...h_h' and 'next token q', must be >= 8 pt. If any is below, raise the figure's minimum type size and re-verify that the figure still fits the text block without shrinking the primary labels.

figure: Figure 1.1 — color coding of the store path vs. the read path
issue: The read path and the store path are distinguished by hue alone, and the hues used are close in luminance, so the distinction largely disappears in grayscale. The distinction survives only because both paths are text-labeled.
evidence: The 'store K' and 'store V' arrows are mid-gray; the 'read V' and 'read K' arrows and the 'read for attention' box are green; the 'stored K - keys' and 'stored V - values' boxes are lavender. A green of roughly (46,125,50) converts to a luminance near 93/255, and a mid-gray arrow near (100,100,100) converts to near 100/255 - a difference of about 3% of full scale, i.e. not perceptible. The lavender box border and the green box border likewise land within a few percent of each other in grayscale. The figure is therefore not self-explanatory in a grayscale print or for a reader with color-vision deficiency, except through the words 'store' and 'read'.
acceptance_test: Convert the figure to grayscale at 300 dpi and confirm that the read path is distinguishable from the store path without relying on hue. If it is not, differentiate by line style (e.g. solid store arrows, dashed read arrows) or by box shape, so that hue becomes redundant rather than load-bearing.

issue: Possible notation collision: 'h' is used here to index attention heads, while 'h' is a common symbol for hidden dimension elsewhere in transformer literature and possibly elsewhere in this manuscript. NOT VERIFIED against the rest of the book (only pages 27-28 were in this batch).
evidence: Figure boxes read 'layer L . h1...h_h'; the caption reads 'each enumerated per head (h1...h_h)'. If the manuscript elsewhere uses 'h' for hidden size (e.g. hidden state h, or a hidden dimension of 8,192 for the canonical dense model), the same glyph denotes two different quantities within one page, which is exactly the kind of drift a reader cannot resolve from context.
acceptance_test: Grep the manuscript for 'h' used as a hidden-dimension symbol and for 'h1...h_h' / 'h_h'. If both exist, rename the head index in Figure 1.1 and its caption (e.g. 'head 1...head H' or 'm1...m_H') and add the chosen symbol to the notation list. If 'h' is not used for hidden size anywhere, close this item with no change.

figure: Figure 1.1 — green box 'read for attention / next token q'
issue: The label conflates the query with the next token and leaves the query's origin unshown, so the box can be read as 'the next token's query is read out of the cache', which is false: the cache supplies K and V only; the query is produced by the projection of the token currently being processed.
evidence: The only two arrows entering the green box are labeled 'read V' (from 'stored V - values') and 'read K' (from 'stored K - keys'). The second line of the box label, 'next token q', sits directly beneath 'read for attention' with no arrow showing where q originates, and the figure has no arrow returning from the attention box to the token column, so the chain terminates without showing that the attention output produces the next token.
acceptance_test: Relabel the box to make the query's role explicit (e.g. 'attention over cached K, V / query q_t from current token') and add an arrow from the token column into the box labeled 'project to q', or a return arrow labeled 'produces next token'. Acceptance: no reader can describe the cache as supplying the query.

figure: Section 1.3 prose immediately above Table 1-1 (worked example)
issue: The worked example's stated token arithmetic is internally inconsistent: the printed operands do not sum to the printed total, and the operand contradicts the canonical scenario, the bullets below it, and Table 1-1 on the same page.
evidence: Printed text: 'If average request is ~2K input + ~300 output = 9.5K tokens per request'. 2K + 300 = 2.3K, not 9.5K. The canonical-scenario sentence two lines above reads 'prompt of ~1,200 tokens plus ~8K retrieved context (~9.2K prompt)'; the bullet below reads 'Input tokens/s: 9,200 tokens/req x 10 req/s = 92,000 tokens/s'; Table 1-1 on the same page lists 'input tokens / request ~9,200' with derivation '1,200 prompt + 8K context'. The only self-consistent reading is 9.2K + 300 = 9.5K, so the operand is wrong, not the total. (Note: at 150 dpi the operand glyphs are small; if the source string is in fact '~9.2K input' and the rendered page is correct, this finding is void - but the source must be checked, because a reader seeing '~2K input' alongside '= 9.5K' will conclude the book cannot do arithmetic.)
acceptance_test: Grep the source for '9.5K tokens per request' and confirm the preceding operand is '~9.2K input'. Then re-derive: 9,200 + 300 = 9,500; 9,200 x 10 = 92,000; 9,200 x 40 = 368,000; 9,200 / 300 = 30.7 (~30x). All four must hold on the printed page. If the source reads '~2K input', rewrite to '~9.2K input + ~300 output = 9.5K tokens per request'.

figure: Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)
issue: The table is split across the page boundary at the foot of printed page 8 with no closing rule visible; the continuation (presumably the tokens/s rows that the prose bullets compute) falls on printed page 9, which was not in this batch. A split table without a repeated header row is a publication-quality defect.
evidence: The last visible row on printed p. 8 is 'output tokens / request | ~300 | canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)', rendered flush to the bottom margin with no bottom rule, indicating the table continues. The header row ('metric | value | derivation') and the caption ('Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)') appear only above the split. The prose immediately preceding the table already states the derived rates (92,000 input tokens/s; 3,000 output tokens/s), so the reader is likely to encounter the table's rate rows only after the rates have been asserted in prose.
acceptance_test: Inspect printed page 9: the continuation must repeat the header row and carry a 'Table 1-1 (continued)' caption, or the table must be rebalanced so it fits on one page. Acceptance: a reader who turns to page 9 sees the header row before any data row.

issue: The caption names a rate ('Token throughput') while the rows visible on the page where the table begins are per-request token counts, not throughput. This is only a defect if the throughput rows are not in the table; if they are (on the continuation page), the caption is acceptable but the split still leaves the caption describing a quantity that is not on the page.
evidence: Caption: 'Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)'. Visible rows: 'input tokens / request ~9,200' and 'output tokens / request ~300'. The word 'throughput' conventionally denotes a rate (tokens/s), which is what the prose bullets compute but what the visible rows do not tabulate.
acceptance_test: After resolving TAB-1.1-03, confirm the caption names the quantities actually tabulated. If the table contains only per-request counts, retitle to 'Token counts per request in the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)'; if it contains both counts and rates, keep the caption but ensure the rate rows are not separated from the caption by a page break.

issue: The derivation cell states the same source twice in two different formats, and the duplication forces an unnecessary line wrap in a column that is otherwise short.
evidence: The cell reads, on two lines, 'canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)' and 'Table 4-2 (1,200 prompt + 8K context)'. The reference 'Table 4-2' appears twice; the second line's informational content is only the arithmetic decomposition '1,200 prompt + 8K context'. The adjacent row's derivation cell uses the single form 'canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)', so the table is internally inconsistent in how it cites the same source.
acceptance_test: Replace the cell with one line: 'canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2): 1,200 prompt + 8K context'. Acceptance: the string 'Table 4-2' appears exactly once per derivation cell, and the row height is reduced to a single line.

issue: The caption contains an unbalanced parenthesis and an orphaned clause, so the sentence that is supposed to define the KV cache's role cannot be parsed without the reader reconstructing the intended structure.
evidence: Printed text reads verbatim: "...and the KV cache is a persistent state — written (append) and read (read past K,V, the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention across steps — not a processing stage." The parenthesis opened after "read (" is never closed; the parenthetical mixes an arrow label ("read past K,V"), an appositive ("the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention"), and the temporal qualifier ("across steps"), and the closing em-dash clause "— not a processing stage" is left syntactically orphaned. This is the caption of the book's first figure and the sentence that establishes the single most consequential distinction in the chapter (cache = persistent state, not a processing stage).
acceptance_test: Rewrite so that every parenthesis balances and each clause has one owner, e.g.: "...and the KV cache is a persistent state — written (the 'append K,V' arrow) and read (the 'read past K,V' arrow, which returns past K/V to attention) across steps — not a processing stage." Verify by re-reading the caption aloud for grammatical closure and by confirming that no '(' remains unmatched in the caption source.

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — edge label on the Embedding → Attention arrow
issue: The forward edge from Embedding to Attention is labeled "attend", which misattributes the attention operation to the wrong edge and invites a reading that contradicts the caption's own insistence that the past-token read path is the backward arrow.
evidence: The Attention box's two sub-lines read "Q,K,V (this token)" and "vs. all past tokens". The only edge carrying past tokens is the green "read past K,V" arrow from KV Cache back into Attention. Labeling the Embedding→Attention edge "attend" therefore suggests that the attending happens on the forward edge, i.e. that the past tokens arrive with the embedding — which is exactly the misconception the caption spends a paragraph disarming ("the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention across steps"). The edge actually carries the current token's hidden state, from which Q (and the current token's K, V) are projected.
acceptance_test: Relabel the Embedding → Attention edge to name what it carries (e.g. "hidden state" or "Q from this token"), leaving "attend" as the operation described inside the Attention box. Confirm that after the change no edge label implies that past tokens enter via the forward path.

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — box sub-labels ("user prompt", "characters", "BPE, byte-level", "corpus-driven", "order = position", "ID to d-dim vector", "one vec/token", "Q,K,V (this token)", "vs. all past tokens", "read + write", "per layer × head")
issue: The box sub-labels appear to be set at roughly 65–75% of the caption's type size, which places them at or below the documented 8 pt print floor for figure in-text annotations. These are the labels that carry the figure's actual content (the per-box qualifiers), so they are the last thing that should be shrunk.

If the caption is set at 9–10 pt, the sub-labels land at approximately 6–7.5 pt. NOTE: this is an estimate from the rendered page, not a measurement of the source font size — the exact value must be confirmed in the figure source or by measuring the built PDF at 100% zoom.

If any annotation is below 8 pt, raise the sub-label size to at least 8 pt and re-check that the box widths still accommodate the longest strings ("ID to d-dim vector", "per layer × head") without clipping or extra wrapping.

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — box fills/borders and the "read past K,V" arrow
issue: Color is used for two incompatible purposes at once, and there is no legend, so the reader cannot infer what the palette encodes. In grayscale the six box fills collapse to near-identical light grays and the palette carries no information at all.
evidence: Green/teal is used both as the fill+border of the Tokenizer and Embedding boxes (i.e. as a "token-space" category) and as the sole distinguishing color of the "read past K,V" arrow (i.e. as "the backward read"). The remaining forward arrows ("split", "emit", "lookup", "attend", "append K,V") are all neutral gray. The six box fills (gray, mint, peach, mint, blue, lavender) all convert to approximately the same light gray value in grayscale, and the borders all convert to similar mid-gray, so in a black-and-white print the only surviving distinction is the bold box title. The figure remains interpretable in grayscale because every box is titled, but the color grouping (Tokenizer/Embedding as a pair) is lost and the green arrow's special status survives only as "slightly darker arrow".
acceptance_test: Either (a) re-color the "read past K,V" arrow with a hue not used by any box, or (b) add a one-line legend stating what the palette encodes, and confirm that the figure remains fully interpretable when converted to grayscale (all six boxes still distinguishable by title, and the backward arrow still identifiable as the only non-gray arrow).

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — left half (Text → Tokenizer → Token IDs → Embedding) vs. right half (Attention → KV Cache)
issue: The diagram silently mixes prompt-level operations with per-token operations without marking where one level ends and the other begins, while the caption describes the whole thing as "the one-token-to-state construction".
evidence: "split", "emit", and "lookup" are prompt-level operations performed once over the whole input (the Text box is labeled "user prompt / characters"). "attend", "append K,V", and "read past K,V" are per-token, per-step operations. The figure title ("How a token travels: text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding → attention → KV cache") therefore describes a chain that changes cardinality halfway across, and the caption's "one-token-to-state construction" gloss does not resolve it. A reader can plausibly infer that the whole prompt is embedded once and then attended as a unit, or that the tokenizer emits one token at a time into the embedding stage.
acceptance_test: Mark the level boundary in the figure — e.g. a light bracket or a small annotation under the Token IDs → Embedding edge reading "per prompt" and under the Attention → KV Cache edge reading "per token, per step" — or state the distinction in one clause of the caption. Confirm that a reader can answer "which of these boxes run once per request and which run once per generated token?" from the figure alone.

figure: Reference to "the figure" in the paragraph beginning "One detail the figure makes explicit is when a token's K/V enters the cache."
issue: The paragraph attributes an explicitness to an unnamed "the figure" that Fig 1.2 does not in fact possess, and the ambiguity is resolvable only by guessing which of the two figures in scope is meant.
evidence: Printed p. 14 opens: "One detail the figure makes explicit is when a token's K/V enters the cache." The paragraph then explains the input-vs-sampled distinction ("A KV token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled") and cites "the green initialize path in Fig 2.1". Fig 1.2 (printed p. 10) shows a single token in isolation and therefore cannot show the input-vs-output distinction at all; that distinction requires the step-to-step loop, i.e. Fig 2.1 (printed pp. 11–13). The nearest preceding figure reference on the page is Fig 1.2, so "the figure" is genuinely ambiguous.
acceptance_test: Replace "the figure" with the explicit figure number ("Fig 2.1") in the first sentence of that paragraph, and confirm that the sentence's claim — that the figure makes the cache-entry timing explicit — is true of the figure actually cited.

figure: FIG 1.2 (p. 10) vs. Fig 2.1 (pp. 11–13, not in this batch)
issue: Possible cross-figure color-semantics collision: green appears in Fig 1.2 as the "read past K,V" (backward read) arrow, while printed p. 14 refers to a "green initialize path in Fig 2.1". If both are green, the same hue encodes two unrelated meanings across two consecutive figures.
evidence: Fig 1.2 uses a distinctly green arrow for the backward read from KV Cache to Attention. Printed p. 14 states: "that first token is the input that seeds the decode loop (the green initialize path in Fig 2.1)". NOT VERIFIED: Fig 2.1 falls on printed pp. 11–13 and was not rendered in this batch, so I cannot confirm its actual color usage. This finding is conditional on that inspection.
acceptance_test: Render and inspect Fig 2.1 (printed pp. 11–13). If its initialize path is also green, either recolor one of the two so that a given hue carries one meaning across both figures, or add a shared legend for the two figures. If the hues are already distinct, close this item with no change.
